title: RFK Jr. tasks researchers with studying vaccine injuries
content: The US Department of Health and Human Services launched a program this week to study and capture the breadth of vaccine injuries, reviving a longtime priority for HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and stoking concerns from some public health advocates. The health secretary unveiled a new vaccine injury research center Monday during a visit to the US National Institutes of Health, where the program will be housed. “Vaccine injury is an invisible disease, and it is purposely invisible,” he said during the event, according to footage shared by HHS. “We have not done the studies that need to be done to understand who’s vulnerable to those kind of injuries.” The announcement also comes with a range of proposals to reform the federal system for reporting adverse events and reimburse doctors who report suspected vaccine injuries, a move HHS said will “encourage” health care workers to make reports. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says on its website that there is a “very remote chance” of vaccines causing serious reactions, injuries or death. But Kennedy’s claims that federal scientists have ignored possible side effects – including debunked theories linking immunizations to autism – have energized his “Make America Healthy Again” base. Last month, Kennedy previewed the proposed changes during a speech before Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine group he co-founded and helped lead before he stepped away to run for the presidency. Kennedy said during the speech that the federal Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System is “very bad” and that although vaccine injuries could be “very rare,” we don’t know under the current system. “In our country, we care about rare illnesses and deaths. We care about every child who dies from measles. They get headlines. We should care about the children — shouldn’t we, I’d ask you, care about children who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries?” he asked the crowd on September 17. Dr. Peter Hotez, co-director of Texas Children’s Hospital Center for Vaccine Development, told CNN that the system the US has in place already works well. “The US already has the most advanced sophisticated system of vaccine monitoring the world has ever seen, with multiple redundant systems in place,” said Hotez, who is also dean of the National School of Tropical Medicine at the Baylor College of Medicine. He pointed to the surveillance system’s ability to pick up “extremely rare side effects of Covid vaccinations” during the pandemic, such as myocarditis in young men who received mRNA vaccines – at a rate of about 1 in 20,000 – and blood clots associated with the Johnson & Johnson vaccine – at a rate of about 1 in 500,000. Hotez said he sees the new moves from HHS as an effort to sow doubt in vaccines at a time when vaccination rates continue to decline, leading to a resurgence in vaccine-preventable illnesses. Pennsylvania is currently the center of the nation’s worst measles outbreak in decades. HHS officials have publicly sparred with state authorities over how many people have died from the disease this year; Pennsylvania has reported five measles-related deaths, all in unvaccinated people, amid more than 1,000 cases across the state. In announcing the vaccine injury actions, Kennedy said it was another bid to restore public trust in health care institutions. Yet Americans’ trust in the CDC has fallen amid Kennedy-led shakeups to the agency, according to KFF polling in February. And most voters, across political parties, said last fall that they felt confident in the childhood vaccine schedule, according to Pew Research Center polling. That polling was done before Kennedy launched a narrowed-down immunization schedule in December and reintroduced the plan this summer. Dr. Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Children’s Hospital of Pennsylvania, said the new HHS initiative gives Kennedy a platform to promote beliefs that haven’t been proved by science. “Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has a bias. His bias is that vaccines cause chronic disease diseases, and it doesn’t matter how many studies show he’s wrong,” Offit said. “Now he’s in a position to be able to create the kinds of studies that fit that bias.”
ranking_reason: The public needs to understand the risks and benefits of vaccines to make informed decisions about their health.

title: The ‘glass skin’ Korean beauty trend has risks, experts warn
content: Greta Costioli was once known as the “ glass skin girl ” on TikTok. Following the Korean beauty trend, Costioli would layer on product after product — toners, serums, essences and moisturizers — in pursuit of an ultra-dewy complexion. Costioli, age 29, said that ever since she was a teenager she would apply extra moisturizer for her naturally dry complexion. When the “glass skin” trend became popular on social media, she fully leaned in, including trying one method requiring seven different layers of hydrating toner. It may sound excessive, but that kind of elaborate skin care routine has become increasingly popular across TikTok and Instagram, where beauty influencers routinely film themselves using skincare products to achieve the glossy, almost reflective complexion known as “glass skin.” Celebrities including Kylie Jenner and Hailey Bieber have amplified the trend, posting their regimens that resulted in similar dewy skin. The glass skin trend has its roots in South Korean beauty culture, where the term is used to describe a complexion that appears exceptionally smooth and pore-less. The phrase appears to have first come around in the early to mid-2010s and then saw a major spike at the end of 2025 going into 2026, according to Google trends . Those who subscribe to the complex routines say their skin benefits from the layers of hydration, and viewers are hooked on the ASMR-like videos as influencers tap their glass-like faces with their fingers and beauty tools. Certain aspects of the glass skin routine, such as moisturizing and using sunscreen, are positive steps toward safe skincare, according to the American Academy of Dermatology. However, problems occur when people use too many products, which can lead to issues such as clogged pores, irritation and breakouts, the association said. Because of the trend’s rising popularity, dermatologists are warning others that the glass skin look may be unrealistic and the skincare routines behind it aren’t suitable for every skin type. Experts also point out that many of the videos contain advice from non-medical influencers, leading to a lack of basic safety information. New research presented September 29 at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) Congress 2026 found that nearly 95% of the most viral videos on the trend contained misleading claims. “We expected to find some gaps in the quality of the information, but I was surprised by how consistent they were,” Dr. Maria Lúcia Paysano, co-lead author of the study and a dermatology resident at the Professor Rubem David Azulay Institute of Dermatology in Brazil, said in an email. The study authors screened the top videos across five Korean skincare-related search terms. After exclusions, 38 videos were assessed for dermatological claims and safety information using the Global Quality Scale and modified DISCERN, a tool used to assess the quality and reliability of health information. Out of the 38 videos analyzed, only one video mentioned irritation risk, two addressed sun protection and none mentioned contact dermatitis risk or advised consulting a dermatologist, according to the study. About 45% recommended combining several active ingredients without safety advice, and 32% promised immediate results. Overall, none of the videos were produced by dermatologists, according to the study. “Problems can arise when complex, one-size-fits-all routines encourage the use of multiple active ingredients without considering individual skin type, tolerance or irritation risk. A skincare routine should prioritize skin health and barrier function rather than simply trying to reproduce a viral appearance,” Paysano said. The bottom line is you can take it too far. For Costioli, who posts her skincare journey on social media, her glass skin routine initially worked well for her, but soon she started having adverse reactions. “At first my skin really loved it, because I have dry skin and my skin absorbs skincare really well. I got a lot of compliments from people online and offline on how great my skin looked,” Costioli said in an email. “However, I kept compromising my skin barrier quite often, because I was simply using too many products.” For her, a broken skin barrier looked like small red bumps on her face that would last for a few days. But if she continued with the extensive routines, the bumps would get more aggressive. “It wasn’t something I could keep up doing, so I had to reduce the steps in my skincare routine,” she said. Experts agree that Korean skincare is not the problem. The concern is that social media can turn simple skincare practices into trendy and complex routines that may not work safely for everyone. “The proof is in the pudding: none of these videos were created by dermatologists, so it should not be a shock that omissions and misinformation are ensued,” Dr. Mona Gohara, a board-certified dermatologist and clinical professor in the department of dermatology at Yale School of Medicine, said in an email. Gohara, who was not involved with the new study, added that many skincare trends, not just the glass skin, have amplified voices that are not medically trained. Additionally, achieving pore-less skin is not possible, as pores are genetic and do not respond to layering products, said Dr. Jane Yoo, a board-certified dermatologist and Mohs surgeon based in New York City. “When patients try to attain this goal, they may inadvertently be disrupting their skin cycle as the physiologic exfoliation signals are now removed,” said Yoo, who is an assistant clinical professor at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. Yoo was also not involved with the study. Common skin issues she observes with her patients who have utilized too many products include contact dermatitis, rosacea and acne flares. Tight, itchy, tender, inflamed, flakey or scaly, and red or darker skin are all signs that someone’s skin barrier may be damaged, added Gohara. To help your skin recover, she recommends pausing scrubs, exfoliating acids and retinoids, and instead cleansing with a gentle, pH neutral, non-soap cleanser and lukewarm water. She added that barrier repair creams can help, and to keep applying sunscreen during the day. “It’s great to have patients educated on their skin but it’s not a one-size-fits-all approach. You have to know your skin type and work with a dermatologist to see if these products are right for you,” added Yoo. The good news is, “you can pursue the glow while taking care of the skin beneath it,” Gohara said. She recommends moisturizing often, especially as skin can become drier with age and hormone changes. To boost that dewy look, layer from lightest to heaviest with a light, concentrated hydrating hyaluronic acid serum, followed by a moisturizer and then a barrier repair cream. Yoo, who is a Korean American dermatologist, often tells patients that they do not need a complex routine for their skin. She typically recommends a four-step approach, including a simple cleanser, an active – such as retinol, Salicylic acid or Vitamin C – a moisturizer and SPF. “The key is to know thy skin and know what it can tolerate,” Gohara said. “Add one product at a time, start slowly, and wear broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher every day. Sun damage is one of the biggest vibrance killers, along with stress, smog, smoking, lack of sleep, and yes sugar.”

title: ‘Cancer is tripling and will keep increasing’: first African to lead global action against disease ready for battle
content: W hen Dr Zainab Shinkafi-Bagudu last saw Gloria in Abuja, the young breast cancer patient was so ill that she was in hospital. The cancer had spread to her bones and lungs, and she was struggling with complications from the disease. Then, at a global conference on cancer thousands of miles away in Hong Kong last month, Bagudu saw her again. Gloria was walking with a stick because of the cancer in her hips, but she was attending sessions, speaking about her experience and advocating for other patients. “I saw her hopping on the corridor here. I was shocked,” Bagudu recalled. Bagudu was recounting this story on the sidelines of the World Cancer Congress in Hong Kong , attended by more than 2,000 people from 124 countries. A Nigerian paediatrician and advocate for cancer patients, Bagudu is president-elect of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) – the first African to lead the organisation. She takes up the role as cancer cases and deaths are projected to rise sharply, with the greatest increases expected in poorer countries. “The fact that it [the election of a black person] took so long is a reflection of the inadequacy of cancer care along the entire spectrum in Africa and other low- and middle-income countries,” Bagudu says. Her election comes as countries across the global south face a growing cancer burden while also struggling with shortages of diagnostic equipment, medicines, radiotherapy services, trained specialists and financing. According to the most recent figures from the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), 20.6 million people were diagnosed with cancer and 9.8 million died from the disease in 2024. The IARC forecasts an annual rise in cases of 67% to more than 34m by 2050 , while deaths could reach 17.5 million, an increase of 79%. Most of the additional deaths are expected to occur in low-income countries. According to Bagudu, the forecasts reinforce the need to reorientate global cancer policy towards countries where health systems are already under pressure. “Cancer is tripling and is going to keep on increasing, and the people affected by it most are those from the global south,” she says. Her ambition is to use the UICC, which represents more than 1,100 member organisations across more than 170 countries, as a bridge between countries with limited cancer services and the research, technology and treatments being developed elsewhere. “I have this opportunity to be able to bring forth a lot of the problems that the low- and middle-income countries are facing to the global north,” she says. But Bagudu says access to cancer care cannot be solved simply by building more specialist hospitals. “We keep building cancer centres and we keep seeing that it’s not enough,” she says. Cancer centres need to be supported by screening, early diagnosis, radiotherapy, medicines, trained health workers and systems that prevent families from being pushed into financial hardship by treatment, she says. “I’m trying to reduce financial toxicity for the woman in the village,” she says. That gap is already visible in basic cancer services. UICC chief executive Cary Adams told delegates that less than half of the world’s population has access to diagnostic services, while many patients in low- and middle-income countries pay for care out of pocket. Only 14% of the estimated 73 million people who need palliative care each year have access to it, according to figures presented at the congress. Bagudu’s own work in Nigeria has focused on some of these gaps. A paediatrician and founder of the Medicaid Cancer Foundation, she helped establish Kebbi state’s first cancer-control plan and registry during her time as first lady of the Nigerian state from 2015 to 2023. Her foundation has also worked on cancer awareness and access to treatment for vulnerable patients. She has campaigned for cervical cancer prevention, including the introduction of the single-dose HPV vaccine into Nigeria’s routine immunisation programme in 2023. In 2024, she became senior adviser to Nigeria’s coordinating minister of health and social welfare with a brief that included women’s health and cancer advocacy. Bagudu now wants to take some of those lessons to the international level, including pushing for new approaches to cancer financing. She says cancer has never received the kind of global treatment financing mechanism that HIV, tuberculosis and malaria have benefited from. “Cancer has never directly been a beneficiary of global funding for treatment,” she says. She will support efforts to develop a global cancer financing platform modelled partly on the Global Fund to Fight Aids, Tuberculosis and Malaria , to mobilise resources from governments, donors and other sources to strengthen cancer prevention, diagnosis and treatment. The proposal comes as African governments face competing demands on health budgets, and international development financing is under pressure with significant cuts to foreign aid . Bagudu also wants greater attention paid to cancers that can be prevented or reduced through interventions already available. She plans to focus particularly on childhood cancers and liver cancer linked to hepatitis. That prevention must go alongside investment in diagnosis and treatment, particularly as cancer risk is shaped by factors including tobacco use, infections, alcohol, diet and obesity, she adds. She wants Africa to have a greater role in cancer research, rather than remaining primarily a recipient of discoveries and training from richer countries. “Research is a little bit more difficult because you have to have the human capacity, you have to have the interest and then you have to have the right environment,” she says. She points to emerging research centres in Nigeria, Rwanda and Kenya, as well as training programmes that bring African health workers to countries including China to develop skills in radiation therapy, cancer technology and other specialist areas. The UICC has set targets including reducing cancer mortality by 25% by 2035, reducing exposure to major cancer risk factors by 30% and ensuring that 60% of cancers are diagnosed at an early stage. Bagudu says the ultimate test of her presidency will be whether the global commitments made in conference rooms reach people far beyond them.
ranking_reason: The election of Dr. Zainab Shinkafi-Bagudu as the first African president-elect of the Union for International Cancer Control highlights the growing cancer burden in low- and middle-income countries and the need for reoriented global cancer policy.
